items.title: 56800_John Simmons oral history interview
items.q: And sometimes Baby Boy -- he was in the band -- he'd let me sit in.

ctx.x: Had you played it in Oklahoma?

I was telling you This Charles Grimm, that had the orchestra there? Every time they would have intermission, I'd grab the bass, you know. And sometimes Baby Boy -- he was in the band -- he'd let me sit in. And at that time, they had this tune, "The Man From Harlem," Cab Calloway, and "White Heat," and "Mule Face Blues." And I'd get up and I'd play it just from having listened to him, you know, from ear. And he just knew that I could play a bass.
So the Wood n Brothers would come if they needed a bass player. So I was so good in his eyesight he would let me check a bass out over the weekend to go and make this gig.

items.title: 56800_John Simmons oral history interview
items.q: Then there was another boy, named Robert Lewis who came out here. He was later known to be called Baby Boy. He worked with Lorenzo Flournoy's trio for a long while.

ctx.x: William Jett. Then there was a orchestra leader at school named Charles Grimm. And I asked him to let me play bass for him, because one boy had graduated from his class, named Rufus -- I can't remember Rufus' last name. He played bass and trombone. He went to Kansas City. And Charles Hadnott-- William Hadnott, what am I saying, Charles Hadnott the bass player that's out here now? He went to Kansas City, he didn't even finish school. He dropped out to go to Kansas City to play bass.
Then there was another boy, named Robert Lewis who came out here. He was later known to be called Baby Boy. He
worked with Lorenzo Flournoy's trio for a long while.
